title: Severe acute malnutrition: inpatient care (India, ICMR and IAP)
subject: paediatrics
setting: Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC), paediatric ward, district hospital
summary: Diagnose SAM by MUAC below 11.5 cm, weight for height below -3 SD or bilateral pitting oedema. Admit to an NRC if there are complications or the appetite test fails; treat hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, electrolytes and infection, then feed cautiously with F-75 before catch-up F-100.

sections.title: Diagnose and triage
items: 6 to 59 months: SAM if MUAC below 11.5 cm, weight for height below -3 SD (WHO standards), or bilateral pitting oedema. Moderate acute malnutrition: MUAC 11.5 to 12.4 cm or weight for height -2 to -3 SD.

Under 6 months (IAP): weight for length below -3 SD, bilateral oedema, or visible severe wasting (use visible wasting if length is below 45 cm). Over 5 years (ICMR): BMI for age -3 SD or below (severe thinness).
Exclude other causes of oedema (nephrotic syndrome, heart failure). Use a digital scale sensitive to 5 g, an infantometer or stadiometer and a non-stretch MUAC tape.

Complications that need admission: poor appetite, lethargy, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, severe dehydration or shock, pneumonia, sepsis, dysentery, severe anaemia, skin infection, jaundice, seizures, untreated TB or HIV.

Appetite test (child not fed for 2 hours, fed by the mother in a quiet place, for 1 hour): passed if a child of 7 to 12 months takes 25 mL/kg or more of F-100, or an older child takes the locally prepared ready-to-eat food: 15 g or more if under 4 kg, 25 g or more if 4 to 7 kg, 35 g or more if 7 to 10 kg.
Triage: SAM with good appetite and no complication: community (home-based) treatment with oral amoxicillin. SAM with complications, poor appetite or failed home treatment: admit to the NRC or ward.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Essential (ICMR): haemogram, random blood sugar, liver and kidney function, chest X-ray, rapid HIV test, gastric aspirate for CBNAAT and AFB.
Desirable: ECG, stool pH and microscopy, urine microscopy and culture, serum sodium, potassium and calcium, serum B12 and folate.
Optional: blood culture, blood gas, and bedside ultrasound (inferior vena cava to aortic ratio) to judge volume status.

sections.title: Stabilisation: hypoglycaemia and hypothermia
items: Hypoglycaemia is blood glucose below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L). Conscious: 50 mL of 10% dextrose, or 1 teaspoon of sugar in 3 teaspoons of water, orally or by nasogastric tube.

Lethargic, unconscious or convulsing: 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg IV, then 50 mL of 10% dextrose or sucrose by nasogastric tube. Recheck glucose after 30 minutes and repeat the bolus if still below 54 mg/dL; if no improvement, treat as shock.
Prevent hypoglycaemia with 2-hourly feeds day and night, starting at once.
Hypothermia: axillary temperature below 35°C or rectal below 35.5°C. Skin-to-skin (kangaroo) care, cap, socks and mittens, warmer or lamp; feed immediately.
Prevent: room at 25°C, no draughts, cover the whole child including head, and change wet clothes or bedding promptly. Hypothermia and hypoglycaemia usually mean serious infection.

sections.title: Dehydration, shock, electrolytes and anaemia
items: Dehydration without shock (IAP): modified low-osmolarity ORS or ReSoMal 5 mL/kg every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, then 5 to 10 mL/kg in alternate hours for up to 10 hours, alternating with F-75. Never full-strength ORS.
Check every 30 minutes for 1 to 2 hours, then hourly. Stop ORS if pulse rises by 15 or respiratory rate by 5, the jugular veins fill or the eyelids become puffy (overhydration).
After rehydration, give 50 mL (under 2 years) or 100 mL (2 years and over) of ORS after each loose stool, and continue breastfeeding more often.

Shock (lethargic or unconscious, cold hands with capillary refill over 3 seconds or a weak fast pulse): transfer to an intensive care facility. IV fluids in SAM are reserved for shock because of the risk of heart failure.

Electrolytes (ICMR): potassium 3 to 4 mmol/kg/day orally for 2 weeks; magnesium 0.4 to 0.6 mmol/kg/day, IM on day 1 then orally for 2 weeks. Cook without added salt; never treat oedema with diuretics.
Transfuse whole blood or packed red cells 10 mL/kg over 3 hours only if Hb is below 4 g/dL, or 4 to 6.5 g/dL with respiratory distress; give furosemide 1 mg/kg IV at the start and monitor closely.

sections.title: Infection and micronutrients
items: Every child with SAM gets antibiotics. Uncomplicated, community treatment: ICMR advises amoxicillin 50 mg/kg per dose twice daily for 7 to 10 days (the IAP STG lists 15 mg/kg 8-hourly for 5 days); follow your NRC protocol.

Complicated SAM (ICMR): ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV or IM 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg IV or IM once daily for 7 to 10 days. If no response in 48 hours or critically ill: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily for 7 to 10 days. Switch to oral amoxicillin 40 to 45 mg/kg per dose twice daily to complete 7 days once feeding.

Add cloxacillin 100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses if staphylococcal infection is suspected (IAP). Diarrhoea for more than 7 days: metronidazole 10 to 12 mg/kg 8-hourly for 7 to 10 days. Dysentery: ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days.
Duration (IAP): clinical sepsis at least 7 days, UTI 7 to 10 days, culture-positive sepsis 10 to 14 days, meningitis 14 to 21 days, bone or joint infection at least 4 weeks.
Vitamin A (ICMR), if food is not fortified: over 12 months 200,000 IU; 6 to 12 months 100,000 IU; under 6 months 50,000 IU.
Zinc 2 mg/kg/day and copper 0.3 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks; folic acid 5 mg on day 1 then 1 mg daily for 13 days (IAP); multivitamin at twice the recommended daily allowance.
Iron 3 mg/kg/day orally only once the child is gaining weight (IAP: after the first 7 days), continued for 6 weeks. No iron in the stabilisation phase.

sections.title: Feeding: F-75 then F-100
items: Stabilisation: F-75 (about 75 kcal and 0.9 g protein per 100 mL) every 2 to 3 hours, at least 5 feeds a day, increasing over 2 to 3 days towards 150 to 200 kcal/kg/day. Record leftovers.
Rehabilitation: switch to F-100 (about 100 kcal and 2.9 g protein per 100 mL) 3-hourly for the next 5 to 7 days, introducing home-available foods, for catch-up growth.
F-75 recipe: 300 mL fresh whole milk, 100 g sugar, 20 mL vegetable oil, water to 1 litre. F-100: 900 mL milk, 75 g sugar, 20 mL oil, water to 1 litre.
Infants under 6 months: same approach, with return to exclusive breastfeeding wherever possible.
Weigh daily at the same time (10 to 11 am) and recalculate feeds. Provide play, sensory stimulation and emotional support, and train the mother to prepare feeds.

sections.title: Monitoring and treatment failure
items: Record pulse, respiratory rate, temperature, urine frequency, stool and vomit volumes, and feeds taken.
Primary failure: no return of appetite by day 4, oedema not starting to resolve by day 4, oedema still present on day 10, or weight gain below 5 g/kg/day for 3 consecutive days on the catch-up diet.

Look for the cause: feeding errors (wrong amount, missed night feeds, leftovers not recorded), unrecognised infection (TB, HIV, UTI), vitamin or mineral deficiency, and then congenital anomalies, inborn errors of metabolism, immunodeficiency, organ dysfunction or malignancy.

sections.title: Discharge and follow-up
items: Discharge from inpatient to outpatient care (ICMR): clinically well and alert, complications and oedema resolving, good appetite taking at least 75% of the 150 to 200 kcal/kg/day target (infants under 6 months gaining 3 to 5 g/kg/day for 3 days).

IAP NRC discharge criteria: weight gain above 15%, weight gain over 5 g/kg/day for 3 consecutive days, oedema resolved, eating adequate home food the mother can prepare, infections treated, micronutrients supplied and immunisation up to date.
Follow up until weight for height reaches -1 SD: at 7 days after discharge, fortnightly in the first month, then monthly.
Teach danger signs: unable to drink or breastfeed, stops feeding, fever, fast or difficult breathing, convulsions, diarrhoea or dysentery.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving IV fluids or full-strength ORS to a SAM child who is not in shock.
Starting iron in the first week.
Treating oedema with diuretics.
Missing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, especially at night.
Withholding antibiotics because the child looks well: infection signs are often absent in SAM.

drugs.name: 10% dextrose
drugs.dose: 5 mL/kg IV if unconscious or convulsing; 50 mL orally or by NG tube if conscious
drugs.notes: For glucose below 54 mg/dL; recheck at 30 minutes.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin (oral)
drugs.dose: Uncomplicated: 50 mg/kg per dose twice daily for 7 to 10 days (ICMR). Step-down: 40 to 45 mg/kg per dose twice daily to complete 7 days
drugs.notes: IAP STG lists 15 mg/kg 8-hourly for 5 days for uncomplicated SAM.

drugs.name: Ampicillin plus gentamicin
drugs.dose: Ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV or IM 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg IV or IM once daily, 7 to 10 days

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: 50 mg/kg IV once daily for 7 to 10 days
drugs.notes: If no response in 48 hours or critically ill (ICMR).

drugs.name: Potassium
drugs.notes: Empirical; do not add salt to feeds.

drugs.name: Magnesium
drugs.dose: 0.4 to 0.6 mmol/kg/day, IM on day 1 then oral for 2 weeks

drugs.name: Vitamin A
drugs.dose: Over 12 months 200,000 IU; 6 to 12 months 100,000 IU; under 6 months 50,000 IU

drugs.name: Zinc and copper
drugs.dose: Zinc 2 mg/kg/day and copper 0.3 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks

drugs.name: Folic acid
drugs.dose: 5 mg on day 1, then 1 mg daily for 13 days

drugs.name: Iron
drugs.notes: Only once weight gain has started (not in the first 7 days).
